voiceover.text: Our survey now asks your name, and where your phone charges overnight. Picture answering honestly. You were scrolling in bed until one in the morning, and your name is right there on the answer. Would you tick the truth? Some people wouldn't, and that changes the data. Collecting data about people comes with responsibilities, to the people and to the results. So what privacy, bias and ethics questions come with a survey like this?

scenes.title: privacy: collect only what you need

voiceover.text: Start with privacy, people's right to control who sees information about them. First, only collect what you actually need. Our question is about sleep, so we don't need anyone's name. Drop it, and the survey becomes anonymous, meaning no one, not even the person running it, can tell whose answer is whose. But be careful. Leaving out names isn't always enough. Say the survey also asks if you're in the band, and if you board at the school. In the band leaves twenty-four students. A boarder in the band, just three. Add that one of them plays the cello. Now that one row, and its four hour answer, belongs to someone everyone can name. So report results for groups, never for one person. If you do need names, say to follow someone up, keep them separate and private. That's called confidential.

Next, ethics, which means treating the people who give you data fairly and honestly. People are doing you a favour, so they need consent, agreeing to take part, knowing what it's for. Tell them what the survey is for, who will see the answers, and that taking part is their choice. They can skip any question, or stop. At school, students under eighteen also need the school's permission, and often a parent's. Don't ask anything that could embarrass or hurt someone for no good reason. And when the results come in, report all of them, including the ones you didn't expect. Reporting only the answers that suit your story is just as unfair as asking an unfair question.

Bias is a lean in the method that pushes results one way. Some of it comes from who you ask, and that's coming up. But a lot comes from how you ask. Here's a leading question, one that hints at the answer it wants. Don't you agree that phones in bedrooms ruin sleep? Ask our twenty students that, and sixteen might agree, just to be agreeable. Now ask it neutrally. Where does your phone charge overnight? Twelve say their bedroom, and eight say somewhere else. That's data we can actually use. Missing options lean results too. If the only choices are bedroom and kitchen, where does everyone else go? And remember the name field. People who feel judged give the answer that sounds good. So privacy isn't just polite. Feeling safe is what makes people honest.

A survey also has to work for everyone in the target population, not just students like the person who wrote it. Our phone question assumes every student has their own phone and their own bedroom. Some share a room, and some don't have a phone. So add options like I share a room, I don't have a phone, and prefer not to say. Some students care for younger siblings, work late shifts, or keep cultural or religious practices that change when they sleep. The survey shouldn't treat any of that as wrong. Some students read English as a second language, or use a screen reader. Plain English, a translation, or a paper copy lets them answer too. And before it goes out, try the survey with a few students from different groups, and fix whatever confuses them. Leave a group out, and the results describe fewer people than you claimed.

scenes.title: putting it together: a survey audit

voiceover.text: Let's audit the whole survey. Do we need every question? The name's gone. Is it anonymous, or at least confidential, and reported in groups? Yes. Does everyone know what it's for, and that they can skip or stop? Yes. Is every question neutral, with an option for every answer? Yes. Does it work for every group in the target population? With the new options, the translation and the paper copy, it does. Five ticks. Now the answers we collect have a fair chance of being true, and of describing the people we said they would.

Here's the card for any survey about people. Ask only what you need. Keep it safe. Ask it fairly. Make it fit everyone. Because people answer honestly when they feel safe, and the question doesn't push them.

Your turn. A gym's survey asks for your full name and mobile number. It also asks, don't you agree our new opening hours are better? Identify one privacy problem and one bias problem, and fix each one. Pause here to answer.

Privacy first. The survey doesn't need your name and number, and they link your answers to you, so drop them, or keep them separate and confidential. Bias next. Don't you agree leads you to say yes. Ask how well the new hours suit you, with balanced choices. Saying it's fine because members agreed to join the gym is the slip.

Last one. A council's survey about a new sports field is online only, it's only in English, and it asks, which sport does your son play? Give two ways it fails to respond to diverse groups, and a fix for each. Pause here to answer.

Online and English only misses people without internet, or with little English, so add paper copies and translations. And your son assumes every household has a son who plays. Ask which sports people in your household play, with none and prefer not to say as options. Saying anyone can open the link is the slip.

Our survey is clear, fair and safe. Now, who gets it? There are two hundred Year 11 students at our school. A hundred and forty live nearby, and sixty catch the early bus, so they get up sooner. We can't easily ask all two hundred, so we'll ask twenty. But which twenty? Pick the wrong way, and the sample won't look like the population. That's next.
